**Surat al-Fatihah**

In the name of Allah, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, the Witness, from whose knowledge nothing is hidden and whose will alone brings anything into being; the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), whose mercy encompasses all existent things, and whose greatness is imprinted upon the mirrors of hearts, so that those glorifications are exalted; whose remembrance is recited upon the tongues in acts of worship and in customary affairs; the Most Compassionate (al-Rahim), whose blessing is complete through His singling out the people of His friendship with the most pleasing of acts of worship.

Our shaykh, the eminent verifier Imam Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-Allamah al-Qudwah Abi Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Allamah al-Qudwah Abi al-Qasim Muhammad al-Mishdali al-Maghribi al-Bijai (Bejaia) al-Maliki, the scholar of his age, may Allah water his grave with clouds of good pleasure and settle him in the highest gardens, said: "The universal principle that yields knowledge of the correspondences (munasabat) between the verses throughout the entire Qur'an is that you consider the purpose for which the surah was brought, and consider what that purpose requires of preliminaries [and consider the ranks of those preliminaries in their nearness to and distance from the goal], and consider, when speech moves through the preliminaries, what it entails of the listener's anticipation toward the rulings and the necessary consequences that follow from it, which eloquence requires to be resolved, removing the burden of that anticipation by making him stand upon them. This is the universal principle governing the linking of all the parts of the Qur'an. If you apply it, the mode of the arrangement (nazm) will become clear to you, God willing, in detail between every verse and verse in every surah and surah. And Allah is the Guide." End of quotation.

It has become clear to me, through my application of this principle after reaching Surat Saba' in the tenth year since I began work on this book, that the name of every surah translates its purpose (maqsud), because the name of everything is the title that shows the correspondence between it and what it names, indicating in summary the detail of what it contains. This is what Adam, peace be upon him, announced when the things were presented to the angels, peace be upon them. The purpose of every surah guides to its correspondence with its name. So I mention the purposes (qusud) of the surah, I match them with its name, and I explain each basmalah in accordance with the purpose of the surah, without departing from the meanings of its words.

The names of al-Fatihah are: "Umm al-Kitab" (the Mother of the Book), "al-Asas" (the Foundation), "al-Mathani" (the Oft-Repeated), "al-Kanz" (the Treasure), [and "al-Shafiyah" (the Healing)], "al-Kafiyah" (the Sufficient), "al-Wafiyah" (the Complete), [and "al-Waqiyah" (the Protective)], "al-Ruqyah" (the Charm), "al-Hamd" (Praise), "al-Shukr" (Gratitude), "al-Du'a'" (Supplication), and "al-Salah" (Prayer). As you see, the core of these names rests upon a hidden matter sufficient for every purpose, namely the watchfulness (muraqabah) which I shall state to be its purpose. Everything that is not opened with it is of no account, and it is the mother of every good and the foundation of every righteous deed. It is not counted unless it is repeated, and so it is constantly recited. It is a treasure for everything, a healing for every disease, sufficient for every concern, complete in attaining every aim, protective from every evil, and a charm for every affliction. It affirms praise (hamd), which is the comprehension of the attributes of perfection, and gratitude (shukr), which is the glorification of the Benefactor. It is the very essence of supplication, for supplication is the turning toward the one called upon. Its greatest assembly of meanings is prayer.

Having established this, the purpose for which al-Fatihah was brought is the affirmation of Allah the Exalted's entitlement to all praises and attributes of perfection, His singling out for the dominion of this world and the Hereafter, and His deserving worship and seeking of help, by asking for the bounty of being directed onto the path of those who attain success, and for rescue from the way of those who perish, His being singled out for all of this. The core of all this is the watchfulness of the servants toward their Lord, by singling Him out for worship. This is the intended purpose of al-Fatihah in itself, and the rest are means toward it. For this requires the affirmation of His encompassing of everything, and that cannot be established until it is known that He is exclusively the Creator, the King, the Owner. The purpose of sending the messengers and revealing the books is the establishment of the laws (shara'i'), and the purpose of establishing the laws is the gathering of creation upon the truth, and the purpose of gathering them is to make them know the King and what pleases Him. This is the purpose of the Qur'an, which al-Fatihah encompasses in the primary intent. That will not be achieved except by what has been mentioned, in knowledge and in action.

* *

Since the purpose of gathering them upon Allah the Exalted is their knowledge of Him for the sake of their worship, and since binding oneself to His name in every movement and stillness leads to watchfulness of Him, calls to awe of Him, and to the belief that the sources and destinations of affairs are from Him and toward Him, the basmalah was prescribed as the beginning of everything, and therefore al-Fatihah is opened with it. The seeking of refuge (ta'awwudh), which belongs to [the averting of] corruptions, was placed before it, glorifying the Qur'an by indicating that it is incumbent upon its reciter to strive to purify his inner self and to gather his scattered affairs, so that he may attain his request and aim from what has been deposited in him of the treasuries of happiness, by turning away from the hostile enemy and turning toward the loving Friend. From here the correspondence between the two protective surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn) and al-Fatihah becomes known.

When the seeking of refuge begins with the letter hamzah, indicating the beginning of creation, and ends with the letter mim, hinting at the return (ma'ad), the basmalah as a whole was made for the return, since it begins with a labial letter (ba'), and the ending of its first word and its last word is with another [labial letter] (mim), indicating that the return to Him in this world is concerned with the management of affairs, even if most of creation is heedless of it; and in the barzakh (intermediate state) it is sensible through death, and in the Hereafter likewise through resurrection. This is what the repetition of the mim concluding its name indicates, by mentioning it twice in it, pointing to the two sensible returns. And Allah knows best. The intended meaning of "name" (ism) here is the supreme attributes.

Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said in his tafsir, in the strange (gharib) words of the basmalah: "The ba' means: what Allah the Exalted made manifest of the wisdom of causation (tasbib). 'Name' (ism) is the manifestation of what is hidden or obscure to the hearts through the medium of the ears, in the form of individuals. 'Allah' is the name of that to which hearts incline when reason stands before it, so it is bewildered (ta'allah) in it, that is, it is perplexed, and it is absorbed (talhu) in Him, that is, it is made independent of everything else through Him. 'Al-Rahman' is the one whose mercy encompasses all that Lordship (rububiyyah) has touched. 'Al-Rahim' is specific to mercy in the manner that Divinity (ilahiyyah) is pleased with." He said, concerning the strange meaning of its words: "When Allah the Exalted made manifest the wisdom of causation and showed creation that some things are derived from other things preceding them, as if they were their causes, some people stopped at the first cause and did not see what came before it, and some stopped at the cause of the cause, up to whatever his intellect might reach. So the Real, the Exalted, folded up those causes and made manifest through the basmalah, that is, through the fronting of the preposition, that everything is by His name and not by any other cause." He said: "He began the Mother of the Qur'an with the basmalah, since its relation to the revealed scriptures and books that preceded it is like the relation of the Mother of the Qur'an to the Qur'an, the book that gathers the scriptures and books, because of the place where it folds up causes. Just as the Mother of the Qur'an contains the secret of the manifestation of actions through the care of the Praiseworthy, the Glorious, in the verse ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. This is in the outward address; beyond that there is an inward meaning, for every verse has an outward and an inward. And creation should adhere to it at the beginning of their words and actions." Thus he said. And more striking than this is that since the relation of the basmalah to al-Fatihah is the relation of al-Fatihah to the Qur'an, al-Fatihah was introduced with it just as the Qur'an was introduced with al-Fatihah. For when it informed of the attribution of all affairs to Him alone, the Glorified, it informed that He alone is the God, and that [is the summary of the detail of al-Fatihah, just as al-Fatihah is] the summary of the detail of the Qur'an in its foundations and branches, its knowledges and subtleties.

Since the name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah, Allah) is a proper name and comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, it was given priority over "al-Rahman" in that it is like a proper name, in that no one else is described by it; and in that it is more emphatic than "al-Rahim," so the more emphatic one was given priority. This accords with the order of existence: origination, then the general blessings, then the special blessings of worship. Both attributes were mentioned as encouragement, and retribution was folded away, in conveying that the second is specific, for the completion of encouragement, by alluding to discouragement.

The intended meaning of the two attributes here is that He, the Glorified, deserves to be described by them by His very essence. He repeated them afterwards as a reminder of the necessity of that for lordship and dominion, and to show that mercy overcame wrath. In the two, together with the encouragement mentioned, is an indication of the rest of the Most Beautiful Attributes, for whoever's mercy encompasses everything cannot have any flaw of deficiency in him. At the end of "Subhan" (Glory be to Him) for this place there is further explanation. The fact that it is nineteen letters in writing and eighteen in pronunciation is an indication that they are drivers of retribution from the Fire, whose guardians are nineteen, and bringers of mercy through the prostrations (rak'at) of the five daily prayers and the rak'ah of the witr, which are among the greatest of the great acts of worship. Since the basmalah is a kind of praise, it is most fitting that it be followed by the name of the universal praise, comprising all its individual forms. It is as if it were said: "Praise Him, for He alone deserves all praises. And single out this kind of praise at the opening of your affairs, because of what has been mentioned of arousing desire toward Him and awe of Him, which leads to adhering to the path of guidance." And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 1, verse 2:

When he established, by his saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾, that He is the one deserving of all praises, not for anything other than His essence, the one possessing all perfections, he indicated that He also deserves it from the standpoint of being a Lord (rabb), a Possessor (malik), a Bestower of blessings (mun'im). So he said ﴿Lord﴾. And by his saying ﴿of the worlds﴾ he indicated the beginning of creation, as an alert to the proofs drawn from the created thing to the Creator, and from the beginning to the return, (p-28) just as he began the Torah with that [li-dhalika]. Al-Harali said: "Al-hamd" (praise) is the complete commendation that encompasses all actions and attributes, given that all of them are from Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, and that all of it is praise, with no blame reaching it. So when the pairing of praise with blame has vanished and the pervasion of praise over the whole is known, it then deserves the manifestation of the name "al-hamd" in its completed form, defined by the word "al" (the definite article), which is a word that, in what it is attached to, indicates its finality and perfection. End of quotation.

Since the station of lordship (al-Rububiyyah) does not gather goodness except through mercy, He followed that with the two attributes ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, encouraging adherence to praising Him. These two attributes contain a repetition, in detail, of what praise (al-hamd) comprehended in principle. The secret of repeating these two attributes will come in al-An'am at ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118]. (p-29) From the Imam Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, that there is no repetition in the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 1, verse 4:

Since the Lord described as Merciful may not be a Owner (*malik*), and lordship (*rububiyyah*) is not complete except with ownership (*milk*), which conveys the complete disposal of affairs, and since the owner may not be a king (*malik*), and his ownership is not complete except with sovereignty (*mulk*), which conveys might (*izzah*) joined with awe (*haybah*), which produces the seizing and subduing that yields the executing of command, He followed that with His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, as a warning against the blows of His glorious majesty.

Al-Harrali said: "The day is the measure in which a manifest matter is completed," (p-30) then he said: "﴿The Day of Judgment﴾ outwardly is the day on which the truth's sole right to enforce recompense becomes manifest, when the claims of the claimants fall away. It runs from the first day of the gathering (*hashr*) to eternal abiding, forever. In reality, it is from the first day on which the recompense takes effect, at the moment of committing a sin, in the inner self of the doer, the trace of the deed, until its final outward completion. This is because recompense does not lag behind the sin, but it is hidden because it occurs in the inner self and its delay in becoming manifest outwardly is not known. For this reason it is related from him, upon him be prayer and peace: 'When the servant commits a sin, a black spot is marked on his heart.'" And also, every punishment that befalls people in this world at the hands of creatures is in truth a recompense from God, although the heedless attribute it to customary causes, as they said: ﴿Adversity and prosperity touched our fathers﴾ [al-A'raf: 95], and attribute it to those who wronged them by their claim. It is, as the Exalted said: ﴿Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. As was also transmitted from him, upon him be prayer and peace: "Fever is from the heat of Hell, and the intensity of heat and cold is from its breath." Fever is the whip of recompense with which all the people of this world are struck, (p-31) and it is the watering-place of the distressing, from which most of them drink without realizing it. He, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Sickness is God's whip upon the earth, with which God disciplines His servants." Likewise is what afflicts them of the torment of the soul in the form of grief, anxiety, restlessness, greed and other things. He, the Exalted, is the sovereign (*malik*) of all of that and its owner (*malik*), whether a claimant claims it or not. He, the Exalted, by the requirement of that, is the Sovereign (*malik*) of the Day of Judgment and its owner absolutely, in this world and the hereafter. To the sovereign the Truth, the Exalted, traced the descent of His lofty command, because by it the matter returned, turning back upon its beginning, with the recompense returning upon the traces of what they were disposed to of qualities that appear upon them in acts, as the Exalted said: ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾ [al-An'am: 139], and ﴿a recompense for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]. And by it the end of the lofty nobility was completed, which is the glory that He expressed by His saying: "My servant has glorified Me." End of quotation. Since there is no difference here in indicating sovereignty between the reading *Malik* and the reading *Malik*/*Malik* [i.e., *Maalik*], the transmission came with both, because when *maalik* (owner) is annexed to *al-yawm* (the day), it conveys its exclusivity with all that is in it of substance and accident, so no one has any command alongside Him and there is no meaning of sovereignty (*malik*) other than this. And since its annexation to the people does not convey this meaning, there was no disagreement regarding ﴿King of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 2].

[p-33] When the matter had gathered together [all the qualities of] deserving, endearment, encouragement, and warning, it was the nature of everyone of understanding to turn toward Him and to concentrate their aspirations upon Him. So He said, turning away from the style of the third person to the second person, and placing the means (al-wasilah) before the request, because it is more fitting for the answering of the prayer: ﴿You alone﴾, that is, O You whose are these attributes! ﴿we worship﴾, as guidance for them to that. The meaning of ﴿we worship﴾, as al-Harali (al-Harali) said, is: we reach the utmost limit in the ways of humbling ourselves. He followed it, repeating the pronoun to emphasize the urgency of seeking help, with ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾, indicating that worship of Him cannot be accomplished except with His help, and that the key to guidance is in His hand. So observe how He, glory be to Him, began with the Essence (al-dhat), then indicated Him through the acts (al-af'al), then ascended to the attributes (al-sifat), then returned to the Essence, as an allusion that He is the First and the Last, the All-Encompassing. When arrival at a portion of the knowledge of the acts and attributes was achieved, the entitlement to being singled out for worship became known, [p-34] and thereupon the inability to fulfil the due right was known, so help was sought. This is like his saying ﷺ, as narrated by Muslim and Abu Dawud in prayer, and al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah in supplication, and al-Nasa'i, and this is its wording, in seeking refuge, from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your punishment, and in Your good pleasure from Your wrath, and in You from You." Then he followed it, in what al-Nasa'i added, with the acknowledgment of inability in his saying: "I cannot count the praises upon You; You are as You have praised Yourself." At the end of Surah Iqra' there is a wonderful explanation of this hadith.

Al-Harali said: These verses, that is, this and what follows it, are among those in which the speech of Allah comes flowing upon the tongues of His creatures, for the whole Qur'an is the speech of Allah. But among it is what is the speech of Allah about Himself, and among it is what is the speech of Allah about what the creatures ought to utter, in the variety of their tongues, their conditions, the ascent of their ranks, and the degrees of their distinction, [p-35] which they cannot reach the reality of because of their deficiency and inability. So Allah, the Trustee over every thing, undertook to inform about them of what was incumbent upon them, which the capacity of His creatures does not reach, and He made their recitation of what He informed about upon their tongues as if it were descending upon them in the station of their having uttered it openly, out of kindness to them and completing His blessing upon them. For if He had left them to themselves in that, they would not have produced anything through which their conditions in their religion and their worldly life could be set right. For this reason they are unable to thank this blessing except that He, may He be exalted, Himself takes charge of it by teaching them of His speech, which becomes the discharge of the right of His favour upon them thereby. And if they cannot inform about themselves of what they owe to their Lord of right, how much less of what would be a report about praising Allah and glorifying Him! So for them there is no [p-36] connection except the recitation of His exalted speech, with understanding or without understanding, and that is their prayer, which is divided, and which [he expressed] in what is authentically related from him, peace and blessings be upon him, of the saying of the Exalted: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves," and then he recited this surah. So the first three verses came with Allah praising Himself, and when the servant recites them, Allah accepts from him the recitation of His servant of His speech and makes it from him as praise, commendation, and glorification. These verses came upon the tongue of His creatures, so their outward meaning is the undertaking of the covenant of worship, which pertains to the servant, and their pillar is the request for help from Allah, glory be to Him, which pertains to the Truth. Thus it was between Him and His servant, and His share was brought forward, because help precedes worship and is realized through it, and He answers what is asked of Him in help. [p-37] Whoever has a burden of some matter and seeks Allah's help in it according to the requirement of this verse, help will come to him according to the measure of his burden. So no one who relies upon the requirement of this verse will ever fall into inability regarding any goal. Inability only occurs through diminishing one's portion from Allah, ta'ala, and ignorance of the requirement of what this verse has perfected, and heedlessness of the blessing in it. And in His saying ﴿we worship﴾, with the nun of accompaniment (nun al-istitba'), there is an indication that the prayer was founded upon collectivity. End of quotation. In the verse there is an exhortation to believe in one's incapacity, to feel one's neediness, and to hold fast to His strength and power. This requires directing one's desires to Him by asking, so He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 1, verse 6:

﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ — an instruction (talqin) to the people of His kindness (ahl luṭfihi), and an alert (tanbih) to the place of the journey (al-sulūk), without which no arrival is possible. As for guidance (al-hudā), al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī) said: it is the return of the one who has gone astray to that from which he strayed. The path (al-ṣirāṭ) is the road whose travelling is dangerous (al-ṭarīq al-khaṭir al-sulūk). The verse is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, spoken on the tongue of the most exalted of His creation. It came completed with the word "al-" (the definite article), because it is the path that no one who is guided along it goes astray from, owing to its all-encompassing nature and the comprehensiveness of its extension, in accordance with the comprehensiveness of the meaning of praise (al-ḥamd) in all existence. It is the path over which opinions have scattered and sects have split by inclining to one of its two sides. Its likeness is set up, and in its manner of meaning, between the two sides of Hell (ẓahrānay Jahannam) on the Day of Recompense, for all to see; and around it, like those opinions, are hooks and grappling-irons (khaṭāṭīf wa kalālīb), by which the states of people in the Hereafter proceed according to how they conducted themselves toward its realities, whose beginning is on the Day of Action. This is the most complete path, the all-encompassing one, which results from straying (al-ḍalāl), by which is expressed the state of one who has no direction (lā wijhata lahu). This straying is praiseworthy (ḍalāl mamdūḥ), because it arises from soundness of nature (salāmat al-fiṭra), for whoever has no knowledge of a direction, his duty is to stop at every direction. And it is a straying that necessitates an all-encompassing guidance from Him.

﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 7]. As for one who has been guided to a direction and then strays from its destination, that is blameworthy straying (ḍalāl madhmūm), because it is straying after guidance, and it arises from crookedness in the disposition (ijtijāj fi al-jibilla). Ended.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glory be to Him, emphasised the report that this (guidance) would come only through His bounty, alerting by this emphasis, which the substitution (al-ibdal, the grammatical construction of apposition) conveys, to the greatness of this path. So He said: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾. Thereby He indicated that holding fast to it means following His messengers. Since He, glory be to Him, bestows favour generally upon every existent, whether enemy or friend, and since omitting the one who bestows (the agent of the favour) in order to intend generality is a case of reducing the wording to multiply the meaning, it was known that the object of the request is some of the people of favour, namely the people of special status. That is, if it were said: "Follow the path of the people of Egypt, for example, not the people of Damascus," it would be known that the negated part is not included in the first, because the condition for that is that both items joined by the conjunction follow it, as the grammarians have stated. This is unlike if it were said: "Follow the path of the people of Egypt other than the wrongdoers," for it is then known that the wrongdoers are among them. Here, then, the intention is to define that the favour is general, even if it is only by bringing into existence. And it is known that the one who travels must encounter the path of some of them, who are those upon whom favour has been bestowed, so the request would not be useful at that point. Hence it became known that what is asked for is the path of the people of favour, described by the attribute of the Merciful (al-Rahimiyyah). Souls longed to know them, so He distinguished them by explaining their opposites, as a warning against them. Thus it became known that they are two groups: one group was willed for wretchedness, so it persisted in neglecting action and thereby deserved anger; and another group was not willed for happiness, so it went astray through neglecting knowledge and thus came to ruin. So He said, warning after giving hope, in order to complete faith by means of both hope and fear, defining that favour is general while what is intended by it is what pertains to the people of honour: ﴿not of those who have incurred (Your) anger﴾. That is, those whom You treat in the manner of one who is angry toward the one upon whom His anger has fallen. The word "ghayr" (other than) became definite so that it would be an attribute of "those," by its being added to its opposite. So it was like: "motion is other than stillness." Since what is intended by "ghayr" is negation, because the context calls for it, and since He expressed it without an exceptive particle, this indicates that the speech is constructed from the outset to exclude those who are characterised by the attribute, and to safeguard the speech from conveying that what is lesser and inferior is included, namely ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾. Thus the measure of favour upon the first group is known, and that there is no salvation except by following them, and that whoever deviates from their way, deliberately or in error, is wretched. So let those of resolve gird up the loins of determination and exert the effort of striving in following their traces, to attain the goodly company of their fellowship in their journey and their abode.

Al-Harrali said: ﴿those who have incurred (Your) anger﴾ are those in whom opposition and deliberate defiance have appeared, and such defiance necessitates anger from the Most High and hatred from those below. And ﴿those who are astray﴾ are those who were directed toward the way of guidance but turned away from it without deliberately intending to do so. "Amin" is a word of resolve, derived from security (al-amn). Its meaning is that the one invoked is secure from refusing the one who called upon him, for nothing overcomes Him or prevents Him. It is only fitting for God, because whatever is other than Him is never free of incapacity or prevention. [End of quotation.] It is a sound by which the act "istajib" (answer) is named, and the final term has been linked to the initial term by the first group's observance of the name of God. Thus they gained the fruit of mercy, while those two groups who opposed were among the party of Satan, and retribution seized them. It is known that the composition of the Qur'an, as it is, is inimitable (mu'jiz). For this reason it is a condition that al-Fatihah be recited in prayer, since it is obligatory in its order. So if one were to place something before it or after it, the prayer would not be valid. [And likewise if one were to insert into it what is not part of it, for that disrupts its composition.]

Al-Isfahani said: The Qur'an is inimitable, and the most evident pillar of its inimitability relates to its composition and arrangement. [End of quotation.] The summary is that when those lofty attributes lifted the veils for their addressee and revealed to him, through the loftiness of their glory, the height of their grandeur and the excellence of their praise, the great mysteries of concealment; and when the gardens of generosity shone upon him, and the subtle gentlenesses of their tenderness spread out for him the expanses of kindness and bounty; then they carried him through the deserts of greatness and majesty, folding up for him, in their facilitation, the wastelands of sovereignty and might, and they flashed for him the lightning of retribution from that exalted threshold. He reached the station of annihilation from the perishable, and he was established in the rank of witnessing the permanence of the Everlasting. So he hastened to submit to Him, turning away from all else, judging the other things by what they possess in themselves of nonexistence and transience. So he said: ﴿You alone we worship﴾, and in that state he realised his inability to fulfil that station's due right, so he said: ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾.

Then witnessing unveiled for him, in the presence of the Worshipped, many paths and lofty, distant stations. He saw many states, dark valleys, drowning seas, guiding lights, and other burning fires. He saw for each a people who had been made to travel (that path), coming sometimes in sorrow and sometimes in ease. He knew that there is no salvation except by His guidance, no protection except by His care, no happiness except by His mercy, and no safety except for the people of His favour. So when he shone forth and was illumined, and the places of the secrets were made known to him through the decrees, it was as if he were asked: "What do you seek, and in which direction do you head?" So he said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

When he sought the most noble path, he asked for the best companions, so he said: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾. Since favour may pertain to worldly matters, he specified it, and he sought refuge from those whom he had observed in the wilderness, wandering, lost from the right course, straying or deviating. So he said: ﴿not of those who have incurred (Your) anger, nor of those who are astray﴾.

It has been indicated in Umm al-Kitab, as the scholar Sa'd al-Din Mas'ud ibn 'Umar al-Taftazani al-Shafi'i said, that all favours return to two kinds of bringing into existence and sustaining: first, bringing into existence and sustaining in this world; and second, bringing into existence and sustaining in the abode of perishing and abiding. As for the first bringing into existence, it is by His saying: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, for bringing forth from nonexistence into existence is the greatest nurturing. As for the first sustaining, it is by His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, that is, the Bestower of the great favours and their subtle details by which subsistence is maintained. As for the second bringing into existence, it is by His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, and this is evident. As for the second sustaining, it is by His saying: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ to the end of the surah, for the benefits of that return to the Hereafter.

Then the opening with praise after al-Fatihah came in four surahs, in each of which one of these favours is indicated, in their order. [End of quotation.] What relates to these from the rest of his speech will come at the beginning of each of the four surahs, God willing. This returns to the basic meaning of praise (al-hamd), for its root, in every arrangement, revolves around reaching the ultimate end, and this entails expansiveness, encompassing and circularity, so it entails the bowing of the head. The ultimate end may also entail contentment, which entails gratitude. This will be explained and applied to particulars in Surah al-Nahl, God willing. Then at the beginning of Saba', there will be verification of what people have said concerning it and its relation to gratitude. The secret of the opening has thus become clear, in that its beginning with praise is partial and then total, for every important matter that is not begun with it is maimed (ajdham). It is followed by the praise of the One praised through what has been mentioned of His beautiful names, together with its inclusion of the totality of the meanings of the Qur'an, from theoretical wisdoms to practical rulings. Thus it is the Mother of the Qur'an, for it is its title, while it is the whole of the Qur'an, since what it contains, despite its brevity, is an elaboration and clarification.

Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said in Miftah al-Bab al-Muqfal li-Fahm al-Qur'an al-Munzal (The Key to the Locked Door for Understanding the Revealed Qur'an), at the end of its ninth chapter: "Let us conclude these chapters by mentioning the Qur'an and its contents concerning the Books, its collection, its recitation, its clarification, its sending down, its causing to descend, its wise and clear aspects, its glorious and generous aspects, its great aspects, its return to the Seven Oft-Repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and the Mighty Qur'an, the Mother of the Qur'an, and what it contains. We shall mention all of this in the tenth chapter.

Chapter Ten: On the place of the Mother of the Qur'an within the Qur'an, and the aspect in which the Qur'an encompasses all the Books and scrolls containing all religions.

Know that God, glory be to Him, gathered His great news, in its entirety, about His great affair in the Seven Oft-Repeated, the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, and its treasure beneath His Throne, in order to manifest it at the seal, when the affair of creation is complete and the first praise appears through Muhammad (ﷺ). This is because He, exalted is He, concludes with what He began with, and He did not manifest it before that, because its manifestation would take away the fear of the creatures and erase their disbelief. The building of the Qur'an cannot be completed except with one who stands as the witnessed clarification of the act, so that the matter may be complete in hearing and in sight. And that is for the one who is among His creation, every creature, so that through him He may make clear every matter of His command. Then, between the beginning of the hidden command and the final perfect creation, there is a gradual progression of the creation's growth and the appearance of the affair according to that command, in scrolls after scrolls and books after books. Scrolls are for what changes quickly, books are for what remains and endures for a period, and tablets are for what abides for a time.

In the Torah are God's judgements upon His servants in this world, through the prescribed punishments, calamities, harms and hardships. In the Qur'an there is some of this, as God wills, and what jurisprudence (fiqh) manifests of the prescribed punishments, and the knowledge of the Sufis concerning the reckoning of calamities. In the Gospel are the principles of those judgements, and the announcement that their purpose is not themselves, but what lies beyond them of the affair of the kingdom of heaven (malakut). In the Qur'an there is some of this, as God wills, of what is manifested by knowledge and the wisdom of the heavenly kingdom. In the Psalms is the enchantment of creatures in ecstasy, while they are away from themselves toward their Lord. In the Qur'an there is some of this, as God wills, of what is manifested by good exhortation. Then He brought the affair and the creation to completion from all its aspects, so it became a Qur'an that comprises everything, completing the favour and perfecting the religion,

﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and the verse continues. (The Prophet said): "I was sent to complete the noble qualities of character." And truly, to your Lord is the final end.

The reason the Mother of the Qur'an is superior to the Qur'an is that the purpose of the Qur'an's revelation is detail and comprehensive principles. In it are scattered stars, not arranged in order, one after another. The comprehensive principles in the Mother of the Qur'an are arranged in order, one after another, up to the completion of the seven verses, in a fulfilment with no addition to it and no deficiency from it. Through what it contains of the Lord's self-manifestation, He displayed the form of His self-disclosure from the beginning of sovereignty to the end of praise; and through what is for His servant, He displayed the form of his own attainment from his freedom from error to the guidance of the Straight Path,

﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Duha: 7], and through what is between Him and him, the stability of the very essence of the command and creation. That is the Mighty Qur'an, comprising what the Qur'an contains, the Absolutely Mentioned, through what is in it of that in detail, from its clear aspect, which is what an audible verse is seen to be; and from its glorious aspect, which is what its judgements have been tested as, among the hastened things witnessed and the deferred things known. It knows what it witnessed, so it became known through the certain experience of what has been transmitted in successive reports of past narratives, and what the present effect has witnessed for it, and what recurs with the times of similar and comparable things. And from its generous aspect, which is what the varied forms of His bounty appear in, in what is subtle and great, hidden and manifest. And from its wise aspect, which is what appears in the well-known wisdom of its demands, and the arrangement of the written creation according to the descent of His command. What proceeded gradually and in approximation to understanding, moving from state to state and judgement to judgement, is called tanzil (sending down, gradual revelation). What was brought down from a height to a lower place is called inzal (sending down in one piece). The latter is sending down where there are no intermediaries, and tanzil is where there are intermediaries. Its clarification is where the leading figure who acts upon it manifests it in his deeds and character, and his character is the Qur'an, and his Qur'an is the arrangement of his recitation according to what the occurring events require."

(p-٥١) The last verse revealed was ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [2:281]. Regarding the content of His saying ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [75:17], he (ﷺ) said: "Place it between the verse of the debt and the verse that precedes it." [For] the composition (*kiyan*) of a verse may come first while its recitation (*qur'an*) in the arrangement (*nazm*) comes later than what precedes it. The verse ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ [33:50] is later in composition but earlier in recitation than the verse ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾ [33:52]. Thus the recitation of a command may correspond with the development of creation, and it may not. Allah undertakes the establishing of both. As for the collection, in His heart the relation of its seven comprehensive elements in the Mother of the Qur'an (*Umm al-Qur'an*, i.e., al-Fatihah) to the Qur'an is like the relation of His collecting it in His heart in a single glance to the Mother of the Qur'an, ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾ [54:50]. So it is a collection in His heart, a Qur'an upon His tongue, (p-٥٢) an explanation in his character and actions, a totality in his breast, and a revelation in his recitation.

﴿And those who disbelieved said: Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?﴾ [25:32] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus﴾ [25:32], meaning: thus did We reveal it, except that what is from you is in the position of the lowest heaven in relation to the universe. ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during a blessed night﴾ [44:3], meaning: to the lowest heaven. ﴿And We sent it down in stages﴾ [17:106], and upon his tongue over the span of the days of prophethood.

He (al-Biqa'i) said in his tafsir: "The Qur'an has an inner and an outer, and its outer is Muhammad (ﷺ)." 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "His character was the Qur'an." So Muhammad (ﷺ) is the form of the inner reality of the Surah of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is its inner reality and its outer form. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [26:193] ﴿upon your heart﴾ [26:194].

He also said in his tafsir of al-Fatihah: "The Surah al-Fatihah was the mother of the Qur'an, because the entire Qur'an is detailed from its comprehensive principles. The first three verses encompass every meaning contained in the Most Beautiful Names and the Most High Attributes, so everything in the Qur'an of that kind is a detailing of their comprehensive principles. The three last verses, from His saying ﴿Guide us﴾ [1:6], encompass everything that surrounds the affair of creation in reaching Allah, withdrawing to the mercy of Allah, and detaching from anything other than that. So everything in the Qur'an from it is from the detailing of the comprehensive principles of these, and everything that becomes a link between that and what these apparent (verses) of creation are, and its origin and its standing in truth, is detailed from the verse ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [1:5]." End of quotation.

Among the most beneficial matters in tasting this path is to contemplate the sacred hadith (*hadith qudsi*, a narration in which the words are attributed to Allah) which Muslim narrated in his Sahih (*Sahih Muslim*, one of the authentic collections of hadith), and the authors of the four Sunan collections, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks." When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [1:2], Allah says: "My servant has praised Me." When he says: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [1:3], Allah says: "My servant has extolled Me." When he says: ﴿Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾ [1:4], Allah says: "My servant has glorified Me," and once He said: "My servant has entrusted (the matter) to Me." When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [1:5], He says: "This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾ [1:6–7], He says: "This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks."

And Allah knows best.
